To: Shared/Ops & HR
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: DRAFT — Brian’s brief for Embakasi, Monday 30 November

Brian,

Thanks for taking this on. After six years working together, you know I wouldn’t leave you to guess your way through this. Here’s what we know, what you can say and what to do if the loading stops. This is still a draft for me to review tonight.

The main thing: this is our mess, not theirs. The guys did nothing wrong. They worked, their pay was due on Friday, and we failed to get it to them. Go in owning that, not defending us.

WHAT HAPPENED ON FRIDAY

The bank rejected the whole payment file at 1:52pm on Friday. It covered 212 casuals. A beneficiary-reference field was longer than the bank’s new 20-character limit following its platform upgrade on 25 November. None of the payments in that file went through.

The rejection alert went to the old finance mailbox, and Kevin only saw it after 5pm, when the bank cut-off had already passed. That explains the failure; it doesn’t excuse it. We should have used the right template and picked up the rejection in time.

Kevin proposed paying through M-Pesa bulk instead. Njeri approved that on Saturday morning. She also approved an extra KES 500 for lunch and fare for every casual on the affected list, in the same M-Pesa batch. The company will cover the M-Pesa charges; they are not to be deducted from anyone’s pay.

WHEN THE MONEY IS EXPECTED

Kevin’s realistic estimate is Monday by 11am. That is the current target, not a guaranteed receipt time. We do not yet have confirmation that the money has been sent or received, and we must not speak as though we do.

Peninah has confirmed 198 phone numbers. She could not reach 14 people, mostly the new loaders from the Athi River intake. She will be at Embakasi from 7:30am with the list so they can confirm their numbers face to face. She is bringing her laptop for anyone who wants a printed payslip.

The 14 unreachable numbers do not mean those people have lost their pay or their KES 500. They need a direct route to Peninah to verify their details. Don’t read their numbers out to the group or send anyone’s pay to a number supplied by someone else without verification.

Before speaking to the group, get the latest position from Kevin: what has actually been completed, what is outstanding, and whether 11am is still realistic. Ask specifically how the 14 corrections will be handled and whether they affect the rest of the batch. We don’t have that answer yet, so don’t guess.

WHAT TO SAY TO THE GUYS

Something along these lines, in your own words:

“Morning, everyone. I owe you an apology from management. You worked and your pay was due on Friday. You did nothing wrong. We failed to get the payment through, and I know that has left people with problems at home.

“The bank rejected our payment file because it did not meet the updated format. We also failed to pick up the rejection before the bank closed for payments. No one in that file was paid.

“Payment through M-Pesa has now been approved. Finance’s current target is Monday by 11am. I am not going to give you an earlier time or tell you it is guaranteed when I cannot confirm that. Every person on the affected list will also receive KES 500 for lunch and fare, with the payment, and the company is covering the M-Pesa charges.

“Peninah will be here from 7:30 with the list. Fourteen people still need to confirm their phone numbers with her. Please see her directly if that includes you, or if you need help checking your details.

“I know another promise is not the same as money on your phone. I’ll tell you what has actually been confirmed and come back with an update even if there is no change.”

Don’t follow the apology with “but”. Don’t minimise rent, fare or food worries. Joseph says some people remember being told “tomorrow” for three days. We need to hear that without arguing with them.

WHAT YOU CAN AND CANNOT PROMISE

You can confirm the approved M-Pesa route, the approved KES 500 for each affected casual, company-paid M-Pesa charges, and Peninah’s attendance from 7:30. You can promise to check, report honestly and help resolve individual problems.

You cannot promise payment before loading, before the 9am departure, “by lunch”, or at an exact minute. Monday by 11am must stay clearly described as Finance’s current target until there is firmer confirmation. Remember Mombasa in 2024: the supervisor said “by lunch”, the money arrived at 4pm, and half the shift sat down. We are not doing that again.

Don’t promise additional compensation, cash advances or another payment arrangement that has not been approved. Don’t call everyone paid simply because a batch has been submitted. Get confirmation of successful payments and identify any failures for follow-up.

If the target slips, say so promptly, explain only what is verified and give the next update time. No rolling “just another few minutes”.

MONDAY MORNING: OUMA, LOADING AND THE 9AM DEADLINE

You’ll be there at 5:30. First speak with Joseph and establish the position on the ground. Before the wider conversation, take Ouma aside privately, ideally before the 6am start. He is loud, but he is not a bad man. He has four children and rent to find. Speak to him as someone carrying a real worry, not as a problem to remove.

Tell him the facts, apologise and let him explain what his group needs you to understand. Ask for his help keeping the conversation calm. Don’t ask him to guarantee everyone’s cooperation or make him responsible for management’s failure.

Be straight about the trucks: Kisumu needs to leave by 9am to keep the mill’s offloading slot, while the payment target is 11am. We cannot honestly offer payment before departure. Ask them to load while we work through the payment, but don’t disguise that timing gap or make the money conditional on loading.

IF HIS GROUP REFUSES TO LOAD

The pay and grievance procedure is clear: any stoppage is handled by Operations and HR together. You should not be left making an HR decision alone just because I’m travelling.

If refusal looks likely, WhatsApp me immediately. I’m awake from 4:30. My flight is at 7:05, so reach me before I board if anything changes. We need to agree named HR cover and a working contact before I lose connectivity; Peninah being there for payroll does not, by itself, settle that.

If loading stops:

• Keep the loading area safe and the conversation calm. Don’t turn it into a public confrontation with Ouma.
• Bring Operations and HR together immediately. Listen to the workers’ representatives and record the concerns, the payment information given and what is agreed.
• No dismissal, threats of dismissal or threats about contracts on Monday. That is explicit in the procedure. Don’t let anyone else make those threats on our behalf.
• Explain that grievances normally go through the shift supervisor and then HR within 48 hours, but don’t use that provision to refuse to hear an immediate pay complaint.
• Separate the pay issue from the dispatch decision. Update whoever is managing the Kisumu dispatch and escalate the risk to Njeri early enough to seek an alternative arrangement or a changed offloading slot. Don’t wait until 9am to announce that departure is impossible.
• Agree the next conversation and update time with the group. Record facts, not labels such as “troublemakers”.

I suggest a short progress check at 7:30 when Peninah arrives, a dispatch decision check by 8am, and a further payment update before 9am. Those are times for updates and decisions, not promises that money will have arrived. If Finance has no new confirmation, say exactly that.

Finally, keep individual follow-up going after the main batch. Someone whose number needs correcting or whose transaction fails must not disappear into “everyone has been paid”. Give them a named contact and a clear next update.

You don’t need to win an argument on Monday. We need to apologise properly, keep people safe, give them facts they can trust and get their pay sorted without making another promise we cannot keep.

Achieng
